source.title: Average Path Length: Sparsification of Nonlinearties Creates Surprisingly Shallow Networks
source.citation: Christian H. X. Ali Mehmeti-Göpel et al., 2022
source.authors: Christian H. X. Ali Mehmeti-Göpel; Jan Disselhoff

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present. The title in the text differs from the supplied catalog title.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on partial linearization and retraining that refine claims about training depth and nonlinear capacity, but it does not directly test most listed mechanisms. Its own findings show that training a network with the extracted nonlinear structure from scratch can perform worse than training first and linearizing later.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 tests comparing post-training partial linearization with retraining from scratch using transferred masks. Other reported outcomes about linearizing at different training stages and effective depth/width do not test the listed claim versions. Figure-only values are not reconstructed. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures test accuracy, test perplexity and remaining nonlinear complexity after partial linearization. It does not measure training classification error, depth-induced training degradation, spurious minima in teacher-student networks, initialization effects, learning-rate stability thresholds or batch-normalization speedups. Its nonlinear-advantage results therefore test none of V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly reflects the authors' discussion: they argue that much nonlinear expressivity is unnecessary after training but helps early optimization, and that partial linearization reveals task-dependent core structures. Its blanket scratch-retraining disadvantage needs qualification: Section 4.1.1 explicitly reports no nonlinear advantage on CIFAR-10 with exact or layerwise mask transfer, whereas every tested CIFAR-100 retraining condition underperforms the partially linearized network. The authors' interpretation in terms of worse minima is not established by the reported test-accuracy comparisons alone.
record.recipe_differences: The paper regularizes channel-wise PReLU slopes toward linearity, then evaluates partially linearized networks or retrains from scratch with transferred inactive-unit masks. It does not test the listed original training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported nonlinear advantage depends on dataset difficulty: the authors describe it as nonexistent on CIFAR-10 in the exact and layerwise mask settings, while on CIFAR-100 no retraining setting matches the partly linearized network. They also report a stronger early-versus-late linearization effect on harder datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10, exact and layerwise mask transfer recover the partially linearized network's test accuracy; global transfer fails for ResNet56 without shortcuts. On CIFAR-100, all scratch-retraining conditions underperform their partially linearized comparators.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization advantage of training with more nonlinear units before partial linearization depends on task difficulty and mask distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Later partial linearization yields better final test accuracy or perplexity, with the largest differences early in training and on harder tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonlinear capacity is especially useful during early training even when the final amount of nonlinearity is held fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: After partial linearization, effective width and depth are approximately independent of initial network size at fixed task and regularization strength; remaining nonlinearities cluster in plain networks and are more evenly distributed in residual networks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained networks contain task-dependent nonlinear core structures whose complexity can be much smaller than the original architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, 2023
record.problems: The listed claim concerns training error and optimization mechanisms, while the paper's main table reports test accuracy after partial linearization and retraining. Figure-based stage, depth and width results lack extractable numerical values in the supplied text. In the CIFAR-10 discussion, the authors call the advantage nonexistent for exact and layer-wise mask transfer despite numerical differences from the extracted network.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only results on stage of linearization (Figure 3 and Appendix Figure 23), width/depth sweeps (Figures 7–10 and appendices), and post-training partial-linearization performance curves (Figures 5–6, 10) are not reconstructed as rows because their values are only shown in figures in the supplied text. They do not directly test any listed version's named behavior.

untested.parts: All parts: near-zero training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and effects of size, stopping and regularization on training error.
All parts: teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-local-minimum frequencies and benefits of extra student neurons.
All parts: training-error degradation with increasing plain-network depth, prevention by identity shortcuts, special tanh initialization and normalization-free residual training.
All parts: initialization-dependent training speed and depth, signal and gradient propagation, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
All parts: recovery above initial stability limits, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
All parts: batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All 15 rows mistakenly use the Base column as the partially linearized comparator; the correct comparator is the Linear. column in Figure 2. The recorded accuracy values otherwise match the supplied table. Related figure-only findings are already declared in rows_left_out and do not warrant missing entries for V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: Training from random initialization to near-zero training classification error, including corrupted or random labels; model size, stopping and regularization effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Whether depth increases training error in plain networks and whether identity shortcuts prevent it; special initialization and normalization-free residual training.
Activation-matched initialization, signal or gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Training behavior above stability limits, curvature changes, edge-of-stability behavior and divergence.
Batch normalization's effect on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

rows.subject: ResNet56S
rows.stage_stated: partly linearized after training; retrained from scratch
rows.operation_detail: Retrained with exact transferred inactive PReLU masks; compared with the partially linearized network.
rows.note: The reference is the extracted, partly linearized network; table columns identify Base, Linear., Exact, Layerwise P., and Global P.
rows.check: Test accuracy does not establish any listed version. The partially linearized comparator is 89.2, not 92.7; 92.7 is the original Base accuracy. Exact retraining matches the linearized comparator according to the authors.
